en: Commentary on the Abhisamaya of Śrī Cakrasaṃvara. Homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara.

First of all, the yogin, having sat down in a high place such as a cemetery or a mountain and with his hair loosened, facing south and having placed a pill of the five nectars in his mouth, should bring to mind the meaning of the four syllables of Śrī Heruka: *Śrī* is non-dual gnosis; *He* is devoid of cause;
*Ru* is free from conceptual proliferation (*vyūha*); and *Ka* is not situated anywhere.

Having recited three times, "I am Śrī Heruka for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings," and having resolved that oneself is the two-armed Saṃvara, immediately thereafter—one should recite three times the mantra garland beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ*, which consists of a row of letters and emits five-colored rays, and visualize it as standing encircling [the deity]. Having meditated on the host of deities in the wheel [of the mandala] who have subdued the hosts of arrogant brahmins, he says what should be done:

First of all, one should cultivate [the meditations] by means of the Lord of Yoga who dwells in the four Brahma-abodes. Having performed everything in this way, how is it that this is called "cultivation of the dwelling in the four Brahma-abodes"? It is obtained from the instruction of the Guru and from the words of the Lord of Yoga. With regard to beings of middling capacity, the cultivation of loving-kindness and so forth is concise: "Having extracted all sentient beings from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), I shall establish them in the great bliss that is of a single flavor with suchness. In that context, compassion arises from the extraction of suffering.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arises from establishing others in happiness; equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises from the nature of suchness (*tathatā*); and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) arises from the nature of stable happiness. Furthermore, the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other immeasurables is well known through their extensive treatment. By the word "should be cultivated" (*bhāvya*), all this cultivation is indicated. Now, the preliminary application (*prayoga*) is stated: the resolute conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*) for the sake of destroying the stains of all conceptual constructions; the purification of all bodily activity through the ego-identification with the two-armed Saṃvara; and the indication that the entire world is, from the beginningless beginning, established as the nature of the utterly pure Śrī Heruka.

Through the meditation on *āli* and *kali*, all verbal activity is purified. Through the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), all roots of virtue increase. Since the complete offering of the pure aggregates and so forth becomes a swift cause for awakening, it is said: "Then one should generate the ego-identity of the five aggregates. In this regard, the certainty that [the aggregates] from form up to consciousness are like foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, and an illusion is the meaning of Vairocana and the others being the suchness of all Tathāgatas.

Alternatively, if one has the firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that they are deities such as Vairocana and so forth, their purification is as follows: therein, within form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there are Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva; and within the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and the other aggregates, there is Akṣobhya. These six should be understood by their colors as white, yellow, red, green, white (or red), and black.

Vairocana has his right hand raised with a wheel and his left hand, together with a bell, resting gracefully at his hip. Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi have their right arms raised in a graceful pose holding a jewel, a red lotus, and a crossed-vajra respectively, while their left hands, together with bells, rest at their hearts. Vajrasattva and Vajradhara have their right hands resting gracefully at their hearts holding a vajra, while their left hands, together with bells, rest proudly at their hips.

Herukavajra has his right hand in the vajra-earth-touching mudrā (*vajrabhūsparśamudrā*), and his left hand holding a bell at his hip with pride. "In the eyes," and so forth. As for those established in other tantras: Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Samantabhadra. Here, Mohavajra and the others are to be understood in sequence. They are white, black, yellow, red, dark green, and black in color. Mohavajra has his right hand raised with a wheel and his left hand holding a gracefully swinging bell at his heart.

Dveṣavajra has his right hand resting on his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell with pride. Īrṣyāvajra, Gamavajra, and Mātsaryavajra have their right arms gracefully raised, holding respectively a jewel, a red lotus, and a double-vajra (viśvavajra), while their left hands rest gracefully on their hearts holding bells. Aiśvaryavajra, however, has his right hand resting on his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell with pride.

Pātanī, Māraṇī, Karṣaṇī, and Narteśvarī each have one face and four arms; they are yellow, black, red, and green in color. Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā are the very nature of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*). Their two right hands hold a wheel, a knife, a vajra-knife, a lotus-knife, a sword, and a dagger. Their two left hands hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

Padmajvālinī has three faces—smoky, white, and red—and six arms; she has the nature of the Vajra-Dharmadhātu and is smoke-colored. Her three left hands hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a noose (*pāśa*). Her three right hands are adorned with a hook (*aṅkuśa*), the head of Brahmā (*brahmāmuṇḍa*), and a curved knife (*kartī*). Vairocana has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Vajrasūrya has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Padmanarteśvara has the nature of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Vajrarāja has the nature of the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

In this context, the proof is as follows: Vajrasattva has the nature of the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Akṣobhya has the nature of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). He is Mohavajra because he destroys delusion; Dveṣavajra because he [overcomes] hatred through hatred; Īrṣyāvajra because he destroys envy; Rāgavajra because he destroys all limbs [of existence]; Mātsaryavajra because he destroys stinginess; and Aiśvaryavajra because he bestows all sovereignty. Pātanī and the others accomplish activities that correspond to their names.

Vairocana and the others stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, wearing crowns of matted hair, possessing three eyes, and adorned with the five seals (*pañcamudrin*). The goddesses have their hair loose, are naked, and stand in the *ālīḍha* posture. "Then" means immediately after the purification of the aggregates and so forth. One should contemplate the vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*) and establish it in the directions starting from the east. Above, however, is a lattice of arrows. With the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should consecrate the ground as a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) line. From the radiance of its rays, there arises the vajra-walls and the vajra-canopy.

The sequence of these seven sentences is written here according to the instruction: preceded by snapping the thumb and forefinger of the left hand while reciting the four mantras beginning with *oṃ sumbha ni-sumbha*, one should place [the deities] in order in the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions—[deities] of black, white, red, and yellow colors, possessing great flaming bodies that pervade the cosmic egg and the subterranean realm (*rasātala*).

Simultaneously with those [deities], one should contemplate four ramparts of the same color as them, produced by the light rays of the *sumbha* mantras; and by means of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) staff arising from the syllable *hūṃ* and presided over by that [double-vajra], one should contemplate the ground extending down to the netherworld (*pātāla*), the net of arrows above in the form of five-pronged vajras produced by the light rays of those [vajras], the vajra-fence below that, and the vajra-canopy in their respective places.

Then there are the four goddesses, Kākāsyā and the others, produced from the four mantras beginning with Sumbha; likewise, the four goddesses Yamadāḍhī and the others are produced from the rays of both sets of mantras. These eight have two arms and one face. From below the navel, they have the form of a trident, and on their right side, they hold a vajra and a mallet.

In the left hand, they hold kila-stakes bearing their own forms; having gone forth by means of the yoga of radiation, they bring the hosts of obstructors situated in the ten directions and, having caused them to enter wells near the eight walls of the eight directions produced from the long-sounding utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*, they nail down the host of obstructors while reciting the nailing mantra and hammer them down while reciting the hammering mantra. Through this nailing and hammering, one should contemplate the host of obstructors as being of the single nature of suchness through great bliss.

Furthermore, having again dispelled all remaining obstacles, one should visualize vajra-lotus-circles as a circular enclosure for the purpose of binding the boundary, as those [obstacles] dissolve into the rampart according to the principle of water-drops emerging from the splashing of water. Thus, one should resolve that the world has become entirely free of obstacles, with the vajra-rampart and so forth becoming a single, seamless whole without any joints.

There is no objection to the question of why, immediately after the *Vajrapañjara* and so forth, there is the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) as the purpose of the mantra; for this tantra is intended for those of superior wisdom (*adhimātra-prajñā*), and for such a person, emptiness alone is the supreme protection. If it is asked, "How then is there an external circle of vajras (*bāhya-vajrāvalī*) in the mandala to be drawn externally?"—it is not so; because the very same [process] that constitutes the manifestation of the Blessed One is itself the manifestation of the universal vajra-garland (*viśva-vajrāvalī*) that delimits the circle of the pledge (*samaya-cakra*). "Tataḥ tataḥ" means immediately after the meditation on protection.

"In one's own heart" means in the heart of oneself situated within the protective cage (*rakṣāpañjara*). "By the letter *A*" means upon the moon transformed from that syllable joined with the *anusvāra*. "By the syllable *Hūṃ*" means in the form of Vajradhara. And it is entirely appropriate that Vajradhara has a lunar disc as his seat. "Radiating various rays of light" means emitting five shimmering rays. As for its own color, the *Hūṃ* syllable is visible through the mouth; it is blue in the center and white on the outside. "Having worshipped" means with the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā.

Therein, the Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Mṛdaṅgā, and Murajā goddesses each have one face and four arms; they are blue, yellow, red, and green respectively. Their two principal arms are intent upon playing their respective instruments, while their other two arms hold a vajra and a vajra-bell. The Hāsyā, Lāsyā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā goddesses each have one face and four arms; they are reddish-brown, blue, yellow, and green respectively. Hāsyā has two hands performing the gesture of laughter. Lāsyā holds a vajra and a vajra-bell, her two principal arms performing the proud dance gesture (lāsyābhinaya).

Gītā holds a lute (*vīṇā*) with her two principal arms; Nṛtyā has two principal arms primarily engaged in the gestures of dance (*abhinaya*). As for these [other goddesses], their other two arms—right and left—hold a skull-bowl (*kapāla*) and a staff topped with a skull (*khaṭvāṅga*). Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Dīpā, and Gandhā are white, smoke-colored, flame-colored, and red in hue respectively; they have four arms and one face. In their primary single arm, they hold a flower, an incense burner (*dhūpakaṭacchuka*), a lamp-stand (*dīpayaṣṭi*), and a perfume conch (*gandhaśaṅkha*). In their other three arms, they hold a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a skull-bowl, and a staff topped with a skull.

The [deities of] taste, touch, and phenomena are white, red, green, and white; they have four arms and one face. With their primary right hand, they hold a mirror, a vessel of nectar, a viśvavajra, and the source of phenomena (dharmodaya). In their other three hands, they hold a ḍamaru drum, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

Having praised [the deities] with the eight-line mantras, one should then surrender oneself to them for the sake of uplifting all sentient beings and recite three times the verse beginning with "The Three Jewels are my refuge," for the purpose of the confession of sins and so forth; thus the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) has been explained. Then, with the words "thereafter" (*tataḥ*) and so on, he describes the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*). When the worshipper, the object of worship, and the act of worship are accepted as being mere representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there is the syllable *Oṃ*. "I am pure by nature" (*svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*) is the purification of the subject (*grāhaka*). Again, "furthermore" (*punar bhūyaḥ*).

"One should contemplate the void" means one should abandon even that conceptualization. "Mere mind, indeed, [is] mere mind"—it should remain in the form of sound (*nāda*). "By the cultivation of the accumulations for enlightenment" means it should be understood as being accompanied by the cultivation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which constitutes the accumulation for enlightenment. "Preceded by the recitation of the mantra": the meaning is that one should cultivate emptiness, characterized by the knowledge of mere appearance; thus, "mere appearance is knowledge. This occurs immediately after [the mantra] *oṃ svabhāva...*. This is the meaning.

Immediately after the worship and so forth, having resolved that the worship and other acts are merely dependently originated mind-only, one should meditate on the three syllables of the *Heruka* mantra at one's own head, throat, and heart. One should then cease [the meditation] by reflecting: "All phenomena are devoid of cause; likewise, they are devoid of arising (*utpāda*); they do not abide anywhere. Sentient beings, not knowing all phenomena to be of such a nature, wander in cyclic existence through their grasping at a self, what belongs to a self, and so forth.

Then, having become Heruka, one should generate compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambanā karuṇā*), thinking: "I shall act in such a way that they will come to know all phenomena as they truly are. Reciting the mantra beginning with *oṃ svabhāva* and so forth, one should perceive the three realms as empty. By the power of one's aspiration, that mind remains positioned higher and higher; one should contemplate it in the form of the syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*, which are white, red, and black respectively.

Then, having emanated the deities of the body-wheel from the syllable *oṃ* and performed the welfare of the world, one should liquefy them through meditative union and cause them to enter back into that very same [syllable]. Likewise, the deities of the speech-wheel from the syllable *āḥ*, and the deities of the mind-wheel from the syllable *hūṃ*. Then, one should dissolve the syllable *oṃ* into *āḥ*, *āḥ* into *hūṃ*, *hūṃ* into the letter *ha*, *ha* into its head (*śiras*), the head into the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the half-moon into the drop (*bindu*), and the drop into the resonance (*nāda*).

Having established [the mind] at a magnitude equal to one-hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair, they wander in cyclic existence because they do not realize the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Therefore, thinking, "I shall realize the *dharmatā* and cause others to realize it," one should contemplate that which has become the great seed, having compassion as its objective support. Having recited the mantra beginning with "Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajra... and so forth, [one says] "from *nāda*. "From there" means from emptiness. "Having awakened" means having established one's own mind in the sky in the form of *nāda*. It remains in the form of the support and the supported.

One should contemplate it as situated above the wind-mandala and so forth; this is the brief statement (*uddesa*). Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) is produced from the syllable *yaṃ* and so on. Regarding the term "universal vajra" (*viśvavajra*), its meaning is as follows: it refers to being upon the pericarp of a universal lotus born from the syllable *paṃ* atop Mount Sumeru. Regarding the phrase "the universal lotus with eight petals, complete with pericarp and filaments," the colors of that lotus are stated according to the sequence of the directions: the eastern direction is red like the fruit of the *phala* tree;
the south-eastern direction is dark green like *dūrvā* grass; and the universal lotus is indeed black.

This is the meaning: yellow in the eastern direction and others; dark blue in the southwest; black in the northeast. Regarding the "union of vowels and consonants" (*ālikāliyoga*), it means one should contemplate the lunar disc in the form of the vowel *tvikā* (which stands for the left and right rotations). Thus ends the yoga.

"In the midst of that" means in the center of the moon. The syllable *HŪṂ* is produced from the sequence of the *nāda*. "Having the form of Vajrasattva" means having the form of the Causal Vajradhara. "Emitting various rays of light" means that one should contemplate [the deity] after first performing yoga with the accomplished heroes (*vīra*) and yoginīs residing in the ten directions—having made the world consist of oneself through the emanation of the deities of the five wheels from the mouth and their subsequent reabsorption, and having liquefied them and caused them to enter the *nāda*.

The seed-syllable is the nature of supreme bliss; at that time, being oriented toward that [bliss], its cause is the state of being Vajradhara. Because it is the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) together with the Blessed One, it is the nature of the fruit. Such is the application.

(“Transformed by that”) means transformed by the vajra. “The Vajra of Śrī Heruka” refers to the Blessed One in his entirety, perfected in the form of the Innate (*sahaja*). One should recite the mantra beginning with the three syllables: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. *Oṃ*, [the one who is] the destruction of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence of all phenomena, whose own body is liberation. Adorned with a crown of matted hair because of having accumulated all roots of virtue; having the crest of a garland of skulls because of having arisen from the *dharmadhātu*; and bearing the half-moon because of having the nature of flowing *bodhicitta*.

His crown is adorned by the Viśvavajra because he acts for the benefit of the entire world. His face is distorted due to the abandonment of false views. He is terrifying with fangs bared because he has destroyed the four Māras. Because of his delight in the yoga of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which are the very nature of the five Tathāgatas and the four Goddesses, he is endowed with rays of light such as the "void" (*śūnya*) and the "charcoal" (*aṅgāra*), and is possessed of the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (*śṛṅgārādirasa*). He wears a tiger skin as a garment because he purifies passion and the other afflictions.
The smearing of all limbs with ashes—[or the garland of ashes]—which is the nature of the fifty letters of the *āli* and *kāli*, indicates the bodhicitta that pervades all limbs.

"In front" means standing while embracing the Blessed One face-to-face. "With a girdle adorned with fragments" means having a waist ornament made from pieces of skull-bowls. "Like the fire at the end of an aeon" is due to the similarity between the nature of emptiness and the non-apprehension of the world. "Of great splendor" is because of the possession of the light of perfectly pure primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). "Possessing a solar halo" means streaming [light] due to the connection with *rajas*. She should be understood as being adorned with the five mudrās. "She encircles" means she remains positioned for the act of climbing a tree.

"Consisting of great bliss and compassion" means that although she is immersed in the great bliss of the nature of insight (*vipaśyanā*), she acts for the sake of the world. The five external signs of the arising of her own bliss are: a slight smile, an embrace, nakedness, disheveled hair, and horripilation.
Having explicitly stated [the worship] for the three genders, the two remaining genders are to be inferred from that;
the goddesses situated in the five-faced [cakra] are established within the five genders.

The purification of the vajra and so forth is described as follows: the black vajra is [purified] by the white syllable *HŪṂ*; its jewel-tip is empowered by the red syllable *VYĀ* (or *DYA*) and the yellow syllable *DYA*. The three-petaled lotus is red and [purified] by the syllable *A*. Its white filaments, which symbolize the heroic bodhicitta, have their tips empowered by the yellow syllable *DYA*. Then, with the mantras beginning with *OṂ VAIROCANĪYA* and so forth, and with the heart and near-heart mantras of the Goddess beginning with *OṂ SARVABUDDHAḌĀKINĪYA*, [one empowers] at the navel and the heart.

Likewise, with the two mantras—the Heart-mantra and the Upahṛdaya-mantra—of his own, the Blessed One should kiss the Blessed Lady on the throat and the forehead; and the Blessed Lady, with the two mantras—the Heart-mantra and the Upahṛdaya-mantra—of the Blessed One, should kiss the Blessed One on the throat and the forehead. Then, one should engage in sexual union (rati) by means of the three-syllable mantra. This same procedure applies even for external beautiful union (śobhanarati).

The first placement of the insignia (*cihnanyāsa*) should be known as being on the left among the goddesses and on the right among the heroes. "Jaṭāmakuṭāṅkapaṭṭakā" means they possess matted locks and crowns (*jaṭāmukuṭin*), and are endowed with the hero’s sash (*vīrapaṭṭa*). "Cūḍā" is a synonym for *rucaka* (an ornament). Since there are two beautiful forms, those facing the intermediate directions have faces like those of monkeys (*mānuṣī*) and are of two colors, but not like the faces of crows and so forth. "Seated upon corpses and most terrible"—this should be understood to apply to all eight. Because they dwell in cremation grounds, these [goddesses] have corpses as their seats. "Of the hero-yoginīs" refers to Vārāhī and the others.

The application of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) is for the sake of abandoning adherence to the appearance of deities and for the sake of seeing the attainment of omniscience. Among these, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the commencement of the full comprehension of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) is the commencement of the full comprehension of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*). The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the determination that the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are like an illusion. The foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is the penetration of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) by way of its own nature.

The basis of psychic power consisting of aspiration (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*) is extreme reverence for the desire to hear the true Dharma and so forth. The basis of psychic power consisting of vigor (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*) is uninterrupted practice in vigor. The basis of psychic power consisting of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda*) is thorough examination. The basis of psychic power consisting of mind (*citta-ṛddhipāda*) is excellence in the direct realization of awakening. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is firm conviction regarding the truths, the Three Jewels, and the fruit of karma; it is the mastery in determining "this is that. The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*) is the determination that [the practice] must necessarily be performed.

The faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya) is the absence of opportunity for ignorance due to the non-forgetfulness of what has been remembered. The faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya) is mastery over one-pointedness of mind. The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is the ascertainment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. These same five faculties, when they have reached the state of ultimate excellence, [are called the powers].

Receiving the designations of the powers of faith and so forth, they are called the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The factor of enlightenment that is concentration is concentration itself as the cause of awakening. The factor of enlightenment that is energy leaves no room for laziness. The factor of enlightenment that is joy is an intense delight in what is wholesome. The factor of enlightenment that is pliancy is the serviceability of the mind toward wholesome action.

The factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga) is the ascertainment that suchness is the intrinsic nature of selflessness. The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-sambodhyaṅga) is the quality of non-forgetfulness. The factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga) is effortlessness within meditative concentration.

Right view is the supreme reverence for the words of the Buddha and the realization of the meaning without error. Right intention is the non-abandonment of the virtuous undertaking once it has been begun. Right speech is discourse that does not deceive sentient beings. Right action is activity that does not transgress the ten wholesome paths of action. Right livelihood is a way of life that does not involve harming sentient beings. Right effort is the application toward the cultivation of the wholesome. Right mindfulness is the recollection of the words of the Buddha. Right concentration is the taking of Śrī Heruka as the object of focus.

The passage beginning with "atha ata" and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding "pīṭha" and so forth, the meaning is that they correspond respectively to the application of the pure seats (*pīṭha*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). In this context, the seats (*pīṭha*), sub-seats (*upapīṭha*), and so on, correspond in sequence to: the Joyous (*pramuditā*), the Immaculate (*vimalā*), the Luminous (*prabhākarī*), the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), the Facing (*abhimukhī*), the Far-Reaching (*duraṅgamā*), the Immovable (*acalā*), the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), and the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). Regarding "pūṃ ja" and so forth, here is the instruction.

While contemplating all [the syllables] such as *pūṃ* and *jāṃ* together with their *anusvāras*, one should instantly perceive the locations of the *pīṭhas* and so forth—transformed from the syllables beginning with *pūṃ* and having the form of half-void circles—at the head and other parts [of the body]. Within those *pīṭhas* and so forth, one should perceive the deities residing in those places, transformed into their respective forms and stationed there. "In the ear" means inside the cavity of the ear. In this same way, it should be understood for the mouth, navel, genitals, anus, the space between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the nostrils as well.

*Khecarī* is the designation for those who have gone to heaven; *bhūcarī* for mortals; and *pātālavāsinī* for those who have gone to the subterranean realm (*pātāla*). Just as rivers situated near external sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth provide nourishment through their water, likewise in the body, the channels (*nāḍīs*) provide nourishment to the nails and other parts; thus there is a similarity. Externally, the *vajrapīṭha* is the place known as Mahābodhi and the river Nairañjanā; internally in the body, the *mahāsukhacakra* is the *vajrapīṭha* and the *avadhūtī* is the *nirañjanā*.

In the mouth, the left and right nostrils, and the anus, there are, in order, Kākāsyā and the other gatekeepers (*dvārapālī*). In the left and right ears and the left and right eyes, there are Yamadāḍhī and the others. In the forehead, the throat, the pericarp of the navel-lotus, and the [other] centers, there are the four beginning with Ḍākinī. The locations of the Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*) and the Lady (*bhaṭṭārikā*) are to be understood from oral instruction. Thus, the complete body-maṇḍala should be visualized repeatedly and clearly.

He concludes the very meaning already stated with the words "by means of the distinction of body, speech, and mind. "He shall become a single form comprising heaven, earth, and the netherworld" means that the Blessed One, whose nature is identical to those [realms] such as heaven, becomes—that is, arises—as their very essence. To the question "How so?", he says "by means of the distinction of body, speech, and mind," which amounts to saying that there is the manifestation of the three wheels through both the external and internal [levels]. To the question "Why?", he says "because of the nature of the three syllables."

The syllable *ha* is "one whose own nature arises through the transformation of the sound (*nāda*) consisting of three syllables"—this means [it arises] in the form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Regarding the term *kṣaṭita*: it is characterized by the union with the form of *kṣa* because it is independent of external marks and so forth; since it is produced simultaneously with the Goddess, it possesses the seal (*mudrā*) of the form of *kṣa*. This means that at the very same time as one's own self, one is possessed of wisdom (*prajñāvān*). It is "completely destroyed" (*kṣaṭitā*) by "everything" (*sarvasarveṇa*), because it is produced simultaneously with the deities of the *Kūṭāgāra*, the Heroes (*vīra*), and the Heroines (*vīreśvarī*).

"One who has been wounded should utter the mantra"—this means that the mantra is uttered at the very moment of completion. He states the three mantras beginning with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, and so forth. The verse beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) is the summary statement (*uddeśa*); "swiftly" (*āśu*) means without dependence on the water-offering (*argha*) and other rites. The passage beginning with "now" (*atha*) is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*). Because there is no difference between the mantra and the deity, the letters *oṃ ha*, and so forth, should be visualized as the respective mantras. The colors of Vajrasattva and the others follow their sequence: white, yellow, red, black, red, and green. "A weapon in all limbs" means they are situated within the wheels (*cakra*) and other parts.

The atoms [of the] cloth have the nature of those colors. That very thing is in the *Bhagavatī*: the mantras beginning with *Oṃ Vaṃ* and so forth have red, blue, white, yellow, green, smoky, and grey colors. Alternatively, Vajrasattva and the others should be visualized in the eight locations produced by their respective mantras: Vajrasattva, Vairocana, Padmanarteśvara, Śrī Heruka, Vajrasūrya, and Paramāśva; they are white, yellow, red, black, red, and green in color.

The Vajrin has three faces and six arms; the others have four arms and one face. In his right hands are a vajra and a *ḍamaruka*, and in his left hands are a bell, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. The principal faces of the Vajrin are white, red, and black, respectively. For the others, the objects in the two right hands are a wheel, a lotus, a vajra, a jewel, and a sword, as well as a *ḍamaruka*; in the two left hands, they hold a bell, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. Vārāhī has red, blue, and green faces; in her left hands she holds a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a noose.

To the right are Aṅkuśā, Brahmā, Muṇḍā, Kartidharā, Yoginī, Mohanī, Sañcālanī, Raṇī, Santrāsanī, and Caṇḍikā. They are blue, white, yellow, green, smoky-grey, and ash-colored respectively; they have loose hair, are naked, possess three eyes, and have six arms. In their left hands, they hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a bell; furthermore, in their right hands, they hold a hand-drum and a knife. All of them stand in the *ālīḍha* posture and possess three eyes.

Those here who possess the white lunar mandalas, and others who possess the solar mandalas—having knotted [the thread] with the tips of the two index fingers (or having knotted it with the tips of the knotted index fingers)—this is what is meant: [the deity] being worshipped by the sixteen goddesses beginning with Vīṇā, impelled by the two *mugra* mantras, drawn in by the rays from the seed-syllable of the heart, and having the form resulting from the transformation of the Vīreśvarīs residing in the ten directions of the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*). One should cause [the deity], marked with the syllable *kṣaṭī*, to enter into oneself.

Then, reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ yoga... and so forth, one should apply the heart-mudrās by means of the lotus-turning gesture (*kamalāvarta*). Upon concluding the heart-mudrās, while performing the gesture of embracing, one should consecrate [the deity] with the three previously mentioned mantras beginning with "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ."

Then one should cause the consecration to be bestowed. In this regard, the instruction is as follows: Simultaneously with the summoning of the Wisdom Wheel (jñānacakra), one should visualize oneself as the Samaya-maṇḍala consisting of great bliss, being consecrated by the Vajrayoginīs who have been summoned—those who hold skull-cups and hand-drums filled with the nectar of wisdom, who are honored by the worship of the goddesses such as Vīṇā emerging from the heart-seed syllable, and who, while reciting the passage beginning with "Just as" and ending with "with water," slightly incline their left hands so that streams of the nectar of wisdom fall from the skull-cups.

Having visualized the Tathāgatas produced from the remaining water and the deities upon one’s own head, one should recite the mantra beginning with "Oṃ sarvatathāgata... and so forth. Then, [one assigns] Akṣobhya to the Blessed One; Vairocana to the Blessed Lady; Ratnasambhava to the Ḍākinīs and others situated in the mind, speech, and body wheels; and Amoghasiddhi to those situated in the pledge wheel (samayacakra), namely Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Vairocana.

Then, preceded by worship, one should taste the nectar (amṛta) offered by the Goddess, which is called "rasa," and perform a hymn of praise with the mantras beginning from the heart-mantra up to the eight-pada mantra. Thereafter, one should visualize the mandala as consisting of the five knowledges and the three bodies, resembling a reflection. Following the recitation, the procedure for the bali offering is mentioned; it is to be explained later. Regarding the phrase "nails, teeth, and so forth are Khaṇḍakapālins," the meaning is that the nails, teeth, and so forth have the nature of Khaṇḍakapālins.

He states the purification of the *Brahmasūtras* and so forth, which take the form of mantras and the like, with the words "the root mantra and so forth," indicating this repeatedly. The meaning is that even without assuming the mudrās, the deity may be perceived as the visible fruit through the mere recitation of the mantra. "Root mantra" refers to the *mālāmantra*; it is the "beginning" (*ādi*) because it is the most excellent. "Of the hero" (*vīram*) means belonging to the hero. "Fashioned from the elements" (*dhātukalpita*) means [fashioned from] nails, teeth, and so forth. "With the six of the armor by the hero" (*ṣaḍbhiḥ kavacasya vīreṇa*) means with the six armor-mantras of the Blessed One.

"This mudrā" means the six mudrās. "The mantra of Vajravārāhī" means by the goddess's garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*). "Of all the Buddha-Ḍākinīs" means by this [mantra]: *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. "By the mantra of the six Yoginīs" means by the mantras of the six Yoginīs contained within the armor (*kavaca*). "Of the Yoginīs of the entire wheel" means by the mantras of the deities beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī.

"Mantrayānakaroṭaka" means that here the mantra is compassion (*karuṇā*). "Vairocanī" refers to the mantra *oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With the words beginning with "evam," he explains what is to be done at the time of wandering; he says this by the word "vicintya" (having reflected). Having armored [oneself], there is the "projecting mantra" (*ākṣepamantro*), beginning with *oṃ sumbhanisumbha* and so forth, which is the four-faced mantra. By means of that, one is well-protected through repeated recitation.

"Always being celibate" (brahmacarya) means having performed the continuous contemplation of all phenomena by way of the vow (saṃvara). "One should indeed worship with the eight-line mantra" means that one should worship others with the eight-line mantras. Having seen the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, and having worshipped them with the eight-line mantra through devotion to the vow, one should perform prostrations and so forth; however, at the time of the practice, one should [worship] oneself alone. "The vow of Cakrasaṃvara" means the nature of the three realms, which is non-different from one's own essential form.

Through the application of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), there is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Through the application of the pure seats and so forth of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there is knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*); likewise, through the application ending with the purity of the armor and so forth, there is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—thus it is taught. This is the *atiyoga*.

Now, by means of the great yoga, he speaks of the state of Vajradhara: "Having meditated on Ālikāli in front," and so forth. "In front" means one should first contemplate the moon. "Of that" refers to the moon. "The syllable" refers to the syllable *HŪṂ*. "The supreme state" refers to the seed-syllable of Vajradhara. "One should contemplate it in the form of the deity" means through the transformation of *HŪṂ*. "Body, speech, and mind as the Vajrin" means Vajradhara.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the state of the sound-form (*nādarūpatā*) of the Blessed One as he gradually dissolves, thinking, "He has become beyond the *piṇḍa*. "Mind alone" refers even to the sound of the mind. With the words "inconceivable" (*acintya*) and so forth, he indicates what was previously stated. "That too" (*sopi*) means "even that. "And the mind itself is not perceived" means that even the conceptualization "it is inconceivable" should not arise. The explanation of this is: "one should contemplate" (*cityet*) and so forth. "That too is inconceivable" means that one should contemplate it as being truly inconceivable.

"Retention" (*dhāraṇī*) refers to the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). By all of this, the following is established: while reciting the deity of the wheel—who radiates the five-colored rays of the sequence of vowels and consonants—one issues forth through the right [nostril] via the wind, transforms the three worlds into a wheel, and becomes of one flavor with the primordially accomplished heroes and yoginīs; then, entering through the left [nostril], one visualizes her at the navel as having become a lunar disc in the form of the reality of the reflected image, and therein, suddenly, the syllable *hūṃ*, which has transformed from that lunar seed-syllable, as the Blessed One.

Having visualized [the deity] seated upon a white lotus seat, resembling a painting drawn in the sky, with two arms and one face, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell with his two hands, and in union with the red, single-faced, two-armed Vajravārāhī who holds a vajra and a skull-cup—having thus seen him, one should gradually dissolve the wheel consisting of the three realms into oneself by means of the sound of illusory passion. As for the sequence: the world [is dissolved] into the cremation grounds; the cremation grounds into the outer wheel; and the outer wheel into the body-wheel.

The body-wheel [is absorbed] into the speech-wheel; the speech-wheel into the mind-wheel; and the mind-wheel into the Ḍākinīs and others located in the cardinal directions, and into the Rūpiṇīs and others located in the intermediate directions such as the northeast. The Ḍākinīs and others are each absorbed into the mouths of the Blessed One; and the Blessed One and the Blessed Lady are absorbed into her two-armed form of Prajñā.

And when that entire [syllable] has entered into the melting state of great passion (*mahārāga*), one should perceive the *haṃ* syllable—which consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—transformed by that melting into something resembling a pearl dyed with vermilion; and the *ukāra* in the head, the half-moon in the half-moon, the bindu in the bindu, and the nada as mere nada, having the form of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair. But for one of superior capacity, even that should not be perceived; this is the meaning. Thus is the Mahāyoga.

When weariness arises, one should quickly resolve upon the maṇḍala circle; having seen either the syllable *hūṃ*—white or red—or the *nāda* at the moon in the navel, while reciting the three syllables, one should emanate the five wheels from that *nāda* by means of the exhalation according to the instruction, and having performed the welfare of the world, while reciting [the mantra] once more, one should cause it to enter back into that very *nāda* by means of the inhalation, together with the mantra, according to the principle of drawing in a thread of wool. One should do this again and again. This is *vajrajāpa*.

In the same manner, from that very *nāda*, while reciting the Heart and Sub-Heart mantras, one should mutter the Heart and Sub-Heart mantras as before through the emanation and reabsorption (*spharaṇa-saṃharaṇa*) of the host of Cakrasaṃvara deities. At the conclusion of the recitation of each deity's mantra, there is a respective emanation and reabsorption. This is the *samaya-jāpa*.

With the conceit of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-ahaṅkāra*), one should visualize that the mantra-garland enters one’s own mouth, proceeds through the path of the *vajra* to the lotus, rises by way of the *avadhūtī*, issues from the mouth of the Blessed Lady, enters through the door of one’s own mouth, dissolves into the *nāda*, and then rising again from that, revolves as before; while contemplating this very [process], one should recite the *mālā-mantra*. This is the *dolājāpa* (swinging recitation).

Then, having offered the bali according to the sequence to be described and having performed the ritual procedure, one should dwell in the form of the deity. At the time of the cremation ground bath, one should perform the rite of consecration.

At the time of eating, however, one should instantly contemplate the body as being the nature of the maṇḍala-cakra, offer the *bali* according to the ritual procedure, and empower the *bali* with the three-syllable mantra. Then, having offered it to the guardians of the directions by reciting once the mantra beginning with "Oṃ kha kha khāhī," and having purified the food and other items through the rite of fire and so forth, one should do so preceded by the pride of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-ahaṅkāra*), reciting: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by commitment; I am pure by commitment."

Having fashioned a curved white vajra with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should consecrate it with the mantra *oṃ amṛtodakaḥ hūṃ hūṃ ṭha ṭha trāṃ āḥ khaṃ hūṃ* and satisfy [the deity] by placing the syllable *hūṃ* at the navel while reciting the three syllables (*oṃ āḥ hūṃ*).

At the midday twilight, having entered the meditation chamber and reciting the three-syllable mantra and others, one should instantly visualize the mandala circle; having performed everything as before, one should dwell at ease. At the midnight twilight, having performed everything as at the midday twilight, and having understood all vocal activity to consist of the vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*), one should recite: "Oṃ! Come, come, O Great Hero, teacher of pure speech, you who are the self-arisen nature of emptiness, gnosis, emanation, and withdrawal!"

Having recited from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, followed by *huṃ huṃ phaṭ*, one should bring the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) to mind and go to sleep while resolving that sleep itself is the state of clear light. At all junctions of the day, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra. Furthermore, at the morning junction, having resolved that the maṇḍala circle has arisen from the clear light, one should recite the entire mantra beginning with *oṃ ehyehi* and so forth; then, having risen, one should perform everything as previously described.

The passage beginning with "the form of the deity of the *khaṭvāṅga*" and ending with "is not established anywhere" should be inserted between the mantra "vairocani" and the phrase "whose crest is made of a skull. The "form of the deity" refers to the form of Śrī Heruka; alternatively, it should be understood as the staff of skeletons (*kaṅkāladaṇḍa*), which is the very nature of the *khaṭvāṅga*. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The sound of the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) demonstrates that [all things] are like an echo. The Blessed One, however, has destroyed the nature of objective apprehension (*upalambha-svabhāva*).

The Yoginī is Night because her intrinsic nature is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Nirvāṇa is that which has emerged from the Hero; it is the sixth, created by the mind. The recollection of Nirvāṇa arises from the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). From Nirvāṇa emerges the Gandharva-being; he is established as having the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), his body adorned with the [thirty-two] marks and endowed with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). Because it consists of the nature of mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), it is measured and ascertained as the sixth; thus it is called "the sixth."

Therefore, the meaning is that one should meditate by resolving that the Hero, the Blessed One, is created from mind (*cittanirmita*) and possesses that very nature. Alternatively, *nirvāṇa* is the *dharmadhātu* because it pacifies the afflictions and secondary afflictions. It is a body consisting of gnosis (*jñānamaya*) that has emerged as a performer of the welfare of sentient beings. Because it thoroughly discerns the sixth [element], the *dharmadhātu*, it is "created from mind" in that way; for it speaks in accordance with the minds of those to be trained.

The manifestation of the pure Dharma is displayed in the form of Vārāhī; "pure Dharma" means emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the meaning is that Vārāhī has that as her intrinsic nature. With the words "the mind finds rest," and so forth, he states the visible benefits. "Yogi" refers to the practitioner. "Nirvāṇa" means death. It is "not shown" in the sense that it is not ultimate. The intention is that death is merely the resting of the mind, like going from one house to another. "At the time of passing away" means at the time of death. "Of yogis" refers to the practitioner.

"This so-called 'death' is a conceptual construction"—this is a worldly conceptual construction. "The state of *khecarī*" refers to the state of clear light (*prabhāsvara*). This is what is meant: at the time of death, one should be led into the state of clear light by the heroic Vajrayoginīs, such as Śrī Heruka and Vārāhī, whose hands are busily occupied with various kinds of flowers, incense, banners, flags, and so forth.
The *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara-abhisamaya-vyākhyā* is completed; this is the work of Śāśvatavajra.
